title: The night of the spirit
hookLine: a deeper night, where even our ideas of God are purified

lines: A NIGHT THAT TAKES THEM AWAY.
cards: A kind old man on a cloud. A stern one. A very large grandfather, or a referee with a whistle.
Those are pictures of God a child might draw, and a child can outgrow them.

But John of the Cross says grown-ups carry pictures of God too: God as my cheerleader, God as a rule book, God as the one who'll make my life work out. And he says there's a night in which even those get taken away.

teach.b: First, who it's for. John says the night of the senses is common, and the night of the spirit is for fewer people, those who have already come a long way in prayer. It goes deeper.
The first night weaned us from sweet feelings. This one reaches our understanding, our memory and our will, the very ways we think about God.
Second, the ray of darkness. Look straight at the sun and you see nothing. You're blinded, not by too little light, but by too much.
So when God's light strikes a soul that isn't ready for it, John says, it feels like darkness. He borrows a phrase from an older Christian writer, Dionysius: a ray of darkness. Third, the pain.
John doesn't soften this. People in this night can feel abandoned, dry, even rejected by God, like the writer of Lamentations sitting in the ruins.
Their old ideas of God don't hold up anymore, and nothing has taken their place yet. It's frightening. John says it's also love: God is making room for himself, the real God, not our picture.
Fourth, bigger than your idea. The prophet Isaiah hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts: nor your ways my ways, saith the Lord."
Any idea of God we can hold in our heads, John says, is smaller than God. That doesn't make the ideas useless; the Church's teaching still stands.
But the God it points to is always larger.

teach.h: MY THOUGHTS ARE NOT YOUR THOUGHTS.
teach.b: Losing a picture, for John, isn't losing God. It can be finding him.

how: Catholics who experience long seasons of spiritual darkness are often pointed to the second book of John's Dark Night, usually with an experienced spiritual director, and the Church remembers saints such as Thérèse of Lisieux who described similar nights.

o: the prophet who wept over Jerusalem in Lamentations
the prophet who hears God say his thoughts aren't ours
the early Christian writer who named a ray of darkness

games.q: what's inside the second night — tap the pairs.
p: purifies even our ideas of God
my thoughts are not your thoughts

s: John says the night of the spirit is for everyone who starts praying
he says it's for fewer people, those who have already come a long way.
John says God's nearness can feel like darkness
like looking at the sun: too much light, not too little.
losing a picture of God means losing God
John says it can be finding him, the real God beyond our ideas.

games.q: you've prayed faithfully for years. now your old ideas of God don't hold, and it feels like God has gone. what does John say is happening?
o: God is making room for himself, beyond your ideas.
you need to find a better picture of God right away.
games.why: John says it can be the night of the spirit: painful, but love. God is purifying our ideas so the real God can come in.

practice: Notice one picture of God you carry: the referee, the distant boss, the one who's disappointed in you, the one who owes you a good life. Just see it, then gently set it down, without rushing to replace it.
If you pray, simply say, you're more than this; if you don't, hold the idea that whatever is deepest is larger than your picture of it.

wordCard.voice: Isaiah. The prophet John quotes for this deeper night, where God says his thoughts are not our thoughts, and even our ideas of God are purified. Today's word.
